translationRepairs: Xiao Zike; his nephew Zifan; Xiao Zixian; Xiao Ziyun
Xiao Zike; his younger brother Zifan; Xiao Zixian; Xiao Ziyun
In the heading 弟子範, 弟 is younger brother, not nephew; s0063 later states that Zifan was Zike's sixth younger brother.
Xiao Zike; his nephew Zifan; Zixian; Ziyun
Xiao Zike; his younger brother Zifan; Zixian; Ziyun
The same heading uses 弟, so the literal 'nephew' is a kinship error; younger brother is the accurate rendering.
Zike and his nephew Zifan and the others once came to court to offer thanks on official business. Emperor Wu received them in the Wende Hall and said at his ease, "I wish to speak with you brothers.

Zike and his younger brother Zifan and the others once came to court to offer thanks on official business. Emperor Wu received them in the Wende Hall and said at his ease, "I wish to speak with you brothers.
子恪與弟子範 is Zike and his younger brother Zifan; the emperor's 卿兄弟 in the same sentence confirms sibling address, not uncle and nephew.
Zike and his nephew Zifan and others once entered to give thanks on an affair; the High Ancestor received them in the Wende Hall and said at ease, "I wish to have words with you brothers.
Zike and his younger brother Zifan and others once entered to give thanks on an affair; the High Ancestor received them in the Wende Hall and said at ease, "I wish to have words with you brothers.
弟 in 弟子範 is younger brother; replacing nephew in the literal line restores the kinship required by the Chinese and by 卿兄弟.
There were also those he did not suspect, such as Emperor Ming of Song, who had originally been an undistinguished commoner and was dismissed from office—how could suspicion have preserved him?
There were also those he did not suspect, such as Emperor Ming of Song, who had originally been a mediocre man and was dismissed from office—how could suspicion have preserved him?
本爲庸常被免 means he had been a mediocre man who was dismissed from office. 庸常 does not mean 'commoner', which invents a social rank the Chinese does not state.
In the early years of the Qi state, we too shared bitterness and sweetness; you were trusted as my inner confidants.
In the early years of the Qi state, we too shared bitterness and sweetness, and the innermost confidence was placed in me.

腹心在我 places innermost confidence in the speaker, so the original reversal (the addressees as his confidants) is wrong. The proposal's 'your innermost trust' still blames the young addressees, but s0023 says those brothers were too young to know the founding years. The confidence rested in the speaker, without making the addressees the trusters.
I took advantage of the chaos to inherit Emperor Ming of Song's realm—I did not seize your family's realm.
I took advantage of the chaos to inherit Emperor Ming's realm—I did not seize your family's realm.
The sentence has 明帝 without 宋. Interpolating Song identifies the wrong house: Wu says he succeeded 明帝家, not 卿家, i.e. Qi Emperor Ming rather than the Yuzhang Xiao line.
Moreover, I took advantage of the chaos to inherit Emperor Ming of Song's realm—I did not seize your family's realm.
Moreover, I took advantage of the chaos to inherit Emperor Ming's realm—I did not seize your family's realm.
The literal line likewise invents 'of Song'. 明帝 here is the Qi emperor whose house Wu replaced, as the contrast with 卿家 shows.
On his return he was appointed Director of the Imperial Clan and Superintendent of the Secretariat.
On his return he was appointed Chamberlain for Ceremonials (Guanglu qing) and Superintendent of the Secretariat.
還除光祿卿 is the Guanglu chamberlain (Court of Imperial Entertainments), not Director of the Imperial Clan, which would be 宗正卿. The proposed office is the one named in this unit.
On his return he was appointed Director of the Imperial Clan and Superintendent of the Secretariat.
On his return he was appointed Chamberlain for Ceremonials (Guanglu qing) and Superintendent of the Secretariat.
The literal field repeats the 光祿卿 / imperial-clan error; Chamberlain for Ceremonials (Guanglu qing) restores the office actually written.
Zike's sixteen brothers all served in Liang.
Zike and his brothers, sixteen in all, served in Liang.
兄弟十六人 is a sibling set of sixteen including Zike, so 'Zike's sixteen brothers' overcounts. The proposal's sense is right, but 'sixteen in all, all served' is clumsy; drop the second 'all'.
Zichan was also famous in the Taiping era. He reached the post of Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel, fled the turmoil to Dongyang, and was later killed by bandits.
Zichan was also famous in the Taiqing era. He reached the post of Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel, fled the turmoil to Dongyang, and was later killed by bandits.
太清中 is the Liang Taiqing era, not Taiping. The era name must be Taiqing.
Zichan was also famous in the Taiping era; he reached the post of Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel, fled the turmoil to Dongyang, and was later killed by bandits.
Zichan was also famous in the Taiqing era; he reached the post of Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel, fled the turmoil to Dongyang, and was later killed by bandits.
The literal line makes the same era-name error: 太清 is Taiqing.
The prince loved literary scholars; Zifan was especially favored and was often told, "This is an extraordinary talent of the imperial house."
The prince loved literary scholars; Zifan was especially favored, and the prince often said, "This is an extraordinary talent of the imperial house."
嘗曰 has no new subject after 王愛文學士，子範偏被恩遇, so the prince is the speaker. 'Was often told' reverses attribution.
When the prince died, Zifan was transferred to Consultant and Follower on the staff of the Xuanhui Prince, and Chief Clerk to the Prince of Linhe Zhengde.
When the prince died, Zifan was transferred to Consultant of the Xuanhui General, and Chief Clerk to Zhengde, Prince of Linhe and Protector of the Army.
宣惠諮議參軍 is a consultant post under the Xuanhui general title, not a 'Xuanhui Prince'. 護軍臨賀王正德長史 makes 護軍 a modifier of Zhengde, Prince of Linhe. The replacement restores both offices.
From youth Zifan's talent and reputation were roughly comparable to those of his nephews Zixian and Ziyun, but his bearing and deportment fell short, so their official careers had their differences.

From youth Zifan's talent and reputation were roughly comparable to those of his younger brothers Zixian and Ziyun, but his bearing and deportment fell short, so their official careers had their differences.
弟子顯、子雲 is younger brothers Zixian and Ziyun. Nephew contradicts 弟 and the chapter's sibling identifications.
Zifan from youth had talent and name roughly comparable to his nephews Zixian and Ziyun, but his bearing and deportment fell short, so their official careers had their differences.
Zifan from youth had talent and name roughly comparable to his younger brothers Zixian and Ziyun, but his bearing and deportment fell short, so their official careers had their differences.
The literal 'nephews' is the same 弟 error; younger brothers is required.

That year at the burial of Empress Jian he and Zhang Xu were commissioned to compose the mourning eulogy. Emperor Jianwen read it and said, "Though the burial rites fall short today, this text is still not inferior to those of old."

That year at the burial of Empress Jian he and Zhang Zuan were commissioned to compose the mourning eulogy. Emperor Jianwen read it and said, "Though the burial rites fall short today, this text is still not inferior to those of old."
張纘 is Zhang Zuan. Xu is not a standard rendering of 纘 and misidentifies the colleague named in the Chinese.
After the rebels were pacified, Emperor Yuan posthumously enfeoffed him as Director with the purple ribbon of the first rank.
After the rebels were pacified, Emperor Yuan posthumously honored him as Grand Master of the Palace with Gold and Purple.
追贈金紫光祿大夫 is a posthumous honorific office, not an enfeoffment, and the title is Grand Master of the Palace with Gold and Purple, not a director with a purple ribbon.
Pang reached the post of Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat's Internal Section, and Recorder to the Prince of Xuan city; he died before his father Zifan.
Pang reached the post of Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat's Internal Section, and Recorder to the Prince of Xuancheng; he died before his father Zifan.
宣城 is the commandery Xuancheng. 'Xuan city' is a false segmentation of the place name.
Que in the Taiping era held office as Friend to the Prince of Xuancheng and Right Chief Clerk of the Minister of State.
Que in the Taiqing era held office as Friend to the Prince of Xuancheng and Right Chief Clerk of the Minister of State.
太清中 is Taiqing, not Taiping.
Que in the Taiping era held office as Friend to the Prince of Xuan city and Right Chief Clerk of the Minister of State.
Que in the Taiqing era held office as Friend to the Prince of Xuancheng and Right Chief Clerk of the Minister of State.
The literal line needs both corrections: 太清 is Taiqing and 宣城 is Xuancheng, not Xuan city.
Soon he was again made Sima to the Xuanhui Prince of Wuling but did not take up the post. He was appointed Palace Gentleman and promoted to Director of Palace Affairs and Minister of Justice.

Soon he was again made Sima to the Xuanhui Prince of Wuling but did not take up the post. He was appointed Grand Master of Palace Leisure and promoted to Director of Palace Affairs and Minister of Justice.
中散大夫 is Grand Master of Palace Leisure. Palace Gentleman would be a 郎 title, not this 大夫 rank.

Whether climbing high to the utmost, facing water to send off the returning, wind stirring on a spring morning, moon bright on an autumn night, early geese and first ducklings, blossoms opening and leaves falling—when these come, I respond and each time cannot restrain myself.

Whether climbing high to the utmost, facing water to send off the returning, wind stirring on a spring morning, moon bright on an autumn night, early geese and first orioles, blossoms opening and leaves falling—when these come, I respond and each time cannot restrain myself.
初鷪 uses the oriole/warbler graph (鶯), a seasonal pair with 早雁. Ducklings are not in the Chinese.

As for climbing high to the utmost, facing water to send off the returning, wind stirring on a spring morning, moon bright on an autumn night, early geese and first ducklings, blossoms opening and leaves falling—when these come, I respond and each time cannot restrain myself.

As for climbing high to the utmost, facing water to send off the returning, wind stirring on a spring morning, moon bright on an autumn night, early geese and first orioles, blossoms opening and leaves falling—when these come, I respond and each time cannot restrain myself.
The literal 'ducklings' is the same misreading of 鷪; orioles matches the graph and the poetic stock image.
Xu in the Taiping era held office as Steward of the Heir Apparent's Household, Junior Mentor, and concurrently managed records.
Xu in the Taiqing era held office as Steward of the Heir Apparent's Household, Junior Mentor, and concurrently managed records.
太清中 is Liang Taiqing, not Taiping.
Xu in the Taiping era held office as Steward of the Heir Apparent's Household, Junior Mentor, and concurrently managed records.
Xu in the Taiqing era held office as Steward of the Heir Apparent's Household, Junior Mentor, and concurrently managed records.
The literal era name must likewise be Taiqing for 太清.
He was transferred to Junior Mentor but did not accept the appointment and was moved to Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel.
He was transferred to Junior Mentor, but before he was installed he was moved to Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel.
未拜 here is 'not yet installed' before 徙爲吏部郎, not a refusal. The next move shows the appointment was superseded, not declined.
He was transferred to Junior Mentor but did not accept the appointment and was moved to Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel.
He was transferred to Junior Mentor; not yet installed, he was moved to Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel.
The literal 'did not accept' over-reads 未拜; 'not yet installed' is the formula for an appointment not yet taken up.
In the second year of Taiping he was promoted to Imperial Censor.
In the second year of Taiqing he was promoted to Imperial Censor.
太清二年 is Taiqing 2, not Taiping.
In the second year of Taiping he was promoted to Imperial Censor.
In the second year of Taiqing he was promoted to Imperial Censor.
The literal date repeats the Taiping error for 太清二年.

Ziyun was skilled at imitating Zhong You and Wang Xizhi while slightly varying the character forms.
He himself said he was skilled at imitating Zhong You and Wang Xizhi while slightly varying the character forms.
自雲 is 'he himself said' (自云), not the personal name 子雲. The following 答敕云 continues that self-statement.
Ziyun was skilled at imitating Zhong You and Wang Xizhi while slightly varying the character forms.
He himself said he was skilled at imitating Zhong You and Wang Xizhi while slightly varying the character forms.
The literal field likewise reads 自雲 as Ziyun. It is a verb of self-attribution, not a name.
In the third month of the third year, when the palace city fell, he fled east to Jinling and died of starvation in a monk's room at Xianling Temple, aged sixty-three.
In the third month of the third year, when the palace city fell, he fled east to Jinling commandery and died of starvation in a monk's room at Xianling Temple, aged sixty-three.
晉陵 is Jinling commandery, distinct from the capital 金陵. Bare 'Jinling' lets the two places collapse; adding commandery matches the toponym actually written.
In the third month of the third year, when the palace city fell, he fled east to Jinling and died of starvation in a monk's room at Xianling Temple, aged sixty-three.
In the third month of the third year, when the palace city fell, he fled east to Jinling commandery and died of starvation in a monk's room at Xianling Temple, aged sixty-three.
The literal line needs the same disambiguation of 晉陵 as Jinling commandery rather than the capital.
The Emperor once said to Ziyun, "Zi Jing's writing does not match Xizhi.
The Emperor once said to Ziyun, "Zi Jing's writing does not match Yishao.
逸少 is the courtesy name Yishao. The quotation already keeps 子敬 as Zi Jing, so rendering 逸少 as the given name Xizhi mixes name types the Chinese does not mix.
The High Ancestor once said to Ziyun, "Zi Jing's writing does not match Xizhi.
The High Ancestor once said to Ziyun, "Zi Jing's writing does not match Yishao.
The literal quotation must likewise render 逸少 as Yishao, parallel to Zi Jing for 子敬.
